data.title: Lasertec vs SCREEN stock: Tokyo's 27-point split tests profit plans
data.description:
Tokyo's semiconductor-equipment trade split sharply at Monday's close. Lasertec finished November 2 at ¥40,720, up 8.01% from its October 30 close of ¥37,700, while SCREEN Holdings closed at ¥9,218, down 18.96% from ¥11,375. The difference was 26.97 percentage points. These are Tokyo Stock Exchange regular-session closes at 3:30 p.m. Japan time, as recorded by Yahoo Finance's Lasertec and SCREEN historical price feeds, rather than live quotations.

That extraordinary one-day separation poses a more useful question than which stock "won" Monday: which company's published profit plan asks investors to assume the bigger recovery from the results already delivered? TECHi's reconstruction of the two companies' October 30 filings shows a different kind of hurdle for each. Lasertec must generate ¥109.231 billion of operating profit in its remaining three fiscal quarters to meet its unchanged full-year forecast. SCREEN must generate ¥101.977 billion in its second fiscal half. Those figures are simple differences between company guidance and reported profit; they are requirements implied by management targets, not independent forecasts of what either company will earn.

Two closing prices, two different businesses

The share-price comparison is striking, but the firms do not sell interchangeable equipment. Lasertec specializes in inspection and metrology, including tools for advanced photomasks. SCREEN's semiconductor production equipment business is centered on wafer cleaning. Both have exposure to complex chip manufacturing, but the timing of customer orders, equipment delivery, acceptance, service revenue and profit recognition can diverge. An AI spending cycle can help both without moving their quarterly income statements together.

The releases also cover different fiscal calendars. Lasertec reported the first quarter of its year ending June 2027. SCREEN reported the first half of its year ending March 2027. Comparing their quarterly sales as if they covered the same period would be misleading. The meaningful comparison is the profit still needed within each company's own fiscal year, and the amount of execution investors are buying at Monday's closing price.

Neither company attributed Monday's market move to a particular analyst's interpretation. Investors may have reacted to order commentary, the absence of a guidance change, positioning or other factors. The closes establish the divergence; they do not prove its cause. The published filings establish the arithmetic beneath the investment case.

Lasertec: the order story still has to become recognized profit

Lasertec's October 30 quarterly filing reports ¥40.369 billion of sales and ¥15.769 billion of operating profit in the July-to-September quarter. Sales fell 25.5% and operating profit fell 41.0% from the same quarter a year earlier. Its ¥10.734 billion of profit attributable to owners was down 43.7%. The operating margin was 39.06%, calculated as ¥15.769 billion divided by ¥40.369 billion. That is a strong absolute margin, but the profit decline is too large to ignore because the stock rose.

Management maintained its fiscal 2027 forecast of ¥290 billion in sales and ¥125 billion in operating profit. It also described demand tied to AI data centers, CPUs, GPUs and high-bandwidth memory and said its order outlook exceeded prior assumptions. That provides a plausible reason to examine future equipment demand. It does not guarantee that orders become this year's revenue, that acceptance falls inside the remaining quarters, or that production costs remain unchanged.

Subtracting the reported quarter from full-year guidance leaves ¥249.631 billion in sales and ¥109.231 billion in operating profit for the following three quarters. The required average is ¥83.210 billion of quarterly sales and ¥36.410 billion of quarterly operating profit, or roughly 2.06 times and 2.31 times the just-reported first quarter, respectively. The implied operating margin over that remaining stretch is 43.76%. This is TECHi's original profit bridge, not a management forecast for each quarter.

The timing matters. Lasertec's quarterly filing shows equipment sales of ¥23.849 billion, down 42.9% year over year, while service revenue rose 31.2% to ¥16.011 billion. Services can support the business while equipment deliveries are uneven, but the full-year target still requires a much larger flow of recognized sales and profit than the opening quarter delivered. The strongest bull case is that orders and delivery schedules make the first quarter a poor guide to the rest of the year. The strongest bear case is that order strength arrives later than recognition needed for fiscal 2027, or at lower margins than the forecast implies.

One cash-flow detail also deserves care. The company reported ¥39.102 billion of operating cash inflow for the quarter, but the filing says customer advance receipts were a significant driver. Advance cash is encouraging as a sign of customer commitment; it is not the same thing as already earned operating profit. A forecast built from cash alone would overstate what has been delivered on the income statement.

SCREEN: cheaper on guidance, but a steep second-half ramp

SCREEN's October 30 half-year filing shows ¥308.453 billion of sales and ¥54.523 billion of operating profit for the six months through September. Those numbers rose 12.5% and 17.4% year over year. Profit attributable to owners rose 18.2% to ¥37.656 billion. The company kept its full-year forecast at ¥743 billion of sales and ¥156.5 billion of operating profit, figures also displayed on its investor financial highlights page.

The implied remaining-half hurdle is ¥434.547 billion of sales and ¥101.977 billion of operating profit. That means second-half sales must be 1.41 times first-half sales, while second-half operating profit must be 1.87 times first-half profit. SCREEN's first-half operating margin was 17.68%; the unchanged full-year target implies 23.47% for the second half, a 5.79-percentage-point improvement. A low share price relative to guidance therefore comes with a demanding earnings acceleration.

The semiconductor production equipment segment delivered ¥251.398 billion of first-half sales and ¥57.528 billion of operating profit. The filing points to stronger DRAM and post-sales demand but weaker foundry demand, and regional changes that include more U.S. and Korean sales but less Taiwan sales. Those mixed drivers matter more than a generic claim that all AI capital spending lifts every supplier. Memory spending can support cleaning tools; an adverse foundry mix or delayed acceptance can still disrupt the margin bridge.

SCREEN's headline first-half results were positive, yet the stock fell almost a fifth at the next Tokyo close. The selloff may reflect concerns about expectations embedded in the price before the report, the second-half concentration of guidance, the demand mix, or factors outside the filing. The disclosure itself does not identify a single cause. What can be checked is the scale of the remaining profit required: nearly ¥102 billion in six months against ¥54.5 billion already earned in the prior six.

What Monday's prices imply, and what they do not

A simple valuation check makes the contrast sharper. Lasertec's published fiscal 2027 earnings-per-share forecast is ¥1,003.27. Dividing Monday's ¥40,720 close by that company forecast produces 40.59 times guided earnings. SCREEN's corresponding published forecast is ¥607.72 per share after its stated share-split treatment. Its ¥9,218 close divided by that number is 15.17 times guided earnings. The resulting multiple gap is about 2.68 to one.

Those ratios are deliberately narrow. They are price-to-company-guidance figures at one closing snapshot, not forward consensus multiples, target prices or total-return forecasts. The fiscal years end three months apart, and earnings-per-share estimates can change with business results, shares outstanding, taxes and non-operating items. Debt, cash, capital intensity and the durability of each company's earnings also differ. Price-to-earnings alone cannot rank fundamentally different equipment franchises.

The balance sheets make a debt-driven explanation for the entire multiple gap too simple. At September 30, Lasertec reported ¥110.768 billion of cash and cash equivalents. SCREEN reported ¥196.411 billion of cash and cash equivalents against ¥8.406 billion of interest-bearing debt in its own financial highlights; these are absolute amounts for differently sized companies, not comparable cash per share or enterprise-value multiples. Lasertec reported 94.286 million issued shares including treasury stock, while SCREEN reported 190.760 million on its post-split basis. A raw share-price comparison therefore says nothing about relative market capitalization. Enterprise-value comparisons would need synchronized market capitalizations and a consistent treatment of cash, debt and leases, which this closing-price snapshot does not supply.

The comparison still defines a practical decision. Lasertec commands a much higher price per yen of guided earnings, even though its first-quarter operating profit fell sharply. Investors paying that multiple are effectively betting that order strength converts into the larger sales and profit run rate implied by guidance and persists beyond one fiscal year. SCREEN trades at a lower guided multiple, but the discount is not automatically a bargain when the published plan depends on an almost 87% jump in second-half operating profit from the first half.

At Monday's closing snapshot, the price action favored Lasertec's future-order narrative and punished SCREEN's need to execute its unchanged target. That is a description of market pricing, not proof that either thesis is right. A cheaper multiple can stay cheap or fall further if earnings miss. A premium multiple can remain justified if an inspection tool's orders and margins exceed the market's expectations. Neither outcome follows automatically from the one-day gap.

A conditional forecast for the next reports

The next evidence to watch for Lasertec is whether actual recognized equipment sales and operating profit begin to approach the ¥83.210 billion and ¥36.410 billion quarterly averages implied by the unchanged annual plan. A second quarter far below those marks would leave more of the target concentrated in the final half, raising execution risk. A quarter above them, accompanied by clear order-to-revenue timing and stable margins, would make the 40.59-times guided earnings valuation easier to defend. This is a checkpoint, not a prediction that the shares will rise or fall on a particular date.

For SCREEN, the key question is whether second-half production-equipment deliveries and mix can support the required ¥101.977 billion of operating profit at an implied 23.47% margin. Evidence of rising recognized sales and a margin approaching that level would strengthen the case that Monday's steep selloff went too far. More order intake without timely revenue conversion, or a weaker foundry and regional mix, would leave the full-year target exposed. An updated company forecast would supersede this bridge and require the calculation to be rebuilt.

There is an important counterargument to reading too much into either arithmetic test. Equipment businesses can be lumpy: a few high-value deliveries and customer acceptances can make one quarter look abnormally weak and the next unusually strong. The companies' own schedules and customer behavior may support the planned ramps even when a simple average looks imposing. Conversely, neither company's annual guidance is a guaranteed baseline, and Monday's closing prices may have reflected expectations that were never visible in the filings.

The clear conclusion is narrower and more useful than a one-day winner call. Lasertec needs to turn a stronger order outlook into sharply higher reported profit to justify a premium valuation. SCREEN needs a much stronger second half to validate a lower company-guidance multiple. The 26.97-point price split tells investors the market treats those risks very differently. The next releases will show whether the profit bridges, rather than the closing tape, deserve the last word.

data.title: CIFR stock forecast: first HPC rent meets a $72M operating loss
data.description:
Cipher Digital reported its first high-performance computing lease revenue on November 2, 2026, but its third-quarter filing also showed a $71.9 million operating loss. The company's results put $5.852 million of data-center rent beside $20.849 million of remaining bitcoin-mining sales. The new business is producing revenue; the question for CIFR stock is how quickly it can become large enough to change the consolidated accounts.

That question became more urgent after U.S. trading opened. Google Finance's CIFR quote showed $6.70 at 9:53:50 a.m. Eastern Standard Time on November 2, about 8% below the prior $7.29 close. This is a dated intraday observation, not a closing price or evidence of a single cause for the decline. The useful forecast is an operating threshold: keeping the rest of the quarter unchanged, how much additional rent would be needed to offset the reported operating loss?

The first HPC rent is real, but the scale is still small

Cipher's quarterly income statement separates the two activities. HPC leasing produced $5.852 million in the three months ended September 30, versus zero a year earlier. Bitcoin mining brought in $20.849 million, down from $71.707 million in the prior-year quarter. Total revenue was $26.701 million, down from $71.707 million. The new rent was 21.9% of current-quarter sales; it has not yet replaced the $50.858 million year-over-year contraction in mining revenue.

The direct-cost line is the promising part of the new segment. Reported HPC lease cost of revenue was $0.726 million, leaving $5.126 million after that line, or 87.6% of HPC rent. This is a calculation from the company's reported amounts, not a disclosed segment operating margin. It excludes company-level compensation, overhead, depreciation, financing and future construction costs. Treating that 87.6% as a permanent mature-project margin would be unjustified; the first delivery is a small, early sample.

The same income statement shows why a high direct margin has not yet resolved the equity question. Compensation and benefits were $38.555 million and general and administrative expense $26.359 million. Depreciation and amortization added $18.821 million. The company reported a $71.915 million GAAP operating loss and negative $10 million of adjusted EBITDA. Those are different measures, but both say the new rent has not yet reached a scale that carries the whole enterprise.

A reproducible threshold for the next phase

Here is the static-cost sensitivity. Divide the $71.915 million quarterly operating loss by the new segment's calculated direct margin of 87.6%. That produces roughly $82.1 million of additional quarterly HPC leasing revenue needed to erase the Q3 operating loss if mining revenue, all other revenue and costs, depreciation, and the direct margin were frozen at Q3 levels. Add the $5.852 million already reported, and the implied quarterly rent level is about $88 million, or roughly 15 times the first quarter's HPC rent. The calculation is an analytical hurdle, not company guidance or a prediction of when breakeven will occur.

That hurdle should be read with two cautions. First, additional data halls will bring project expenses and likely more depreciation, so a constant-cost model can make the path look easier than reality. Second, the mining operation is deliberately shrinking; a further fall in mining gross profit would increase the rent needed to compensate. The reverse could also happen: a lower overhead run rate or higher rent yield could improve the bridge. The next two quarterly statements, not the signed headline value of a lease, will show which forces dominate.

A nearer-term checkpoint is adjusted EBITDA. At Q3's negative $10 million, a simple division by the 87.6% direct margin suggests about $11.4 million of incremental quarterly HPC rent would close that particular gap if every other adjusted-EBITDA component stayed fixed. That is a much smaller threshold than GAAP operating breakeven because depreciation and certain other items sit outside adjusted EBITDA. It does not mean $17.3 million of total quarterly rent would make Cipher profitable or cash-flow positive. Investors should ask management to reconcile each new project contribution to both GAAP and cash outcomes.

Why the reported net profit is a poor shortcut

Readers may see a positive Q3 net income figure and think the transition has already succeeded. The reported reconciliation shows $31.596 million of GAAP net income even though operations lost $71.915 million. A $127.180 million gain from the change in fair value of a warrant liability helped bridge that difference. Such a mark-to-market gain can reverse and does not represent rent collected from a customer. It is part of GAAP earnings, but it is not evidence that the data centers have covered their operating burden.

Interest also matters. Q3 interest expense was $58.994 million, against $32.684 million of interest income. The company issued $850 million of zero-coupon convertible notes due in 2032 and equitized most of a smaller 2030 note balance. The zero coupon limits cash interest on that specific issuance, but the consolidated interest line and project financing still need watching. Nor should a share-price forecast turn a large contracted-rent number into today's equity value without accounting for debt, construction spend and the timing of deliveries.

The $9.1 billion lease is a schedule, not Q4 sales

Cipher said the expanded Barber Lake lease has approximately $9.1 billion of contracted revenue over a 20-year term, including about $5.2 billion added in the amendment. The amendment was disclosed in a September 24 filing; repeating the total today does not make the contract itself a new November 2 signing. Dividing $9.1 billion by 20 yields $455 million per year as a simple lifetime average, or $113.75 million per quarter. That average is not the contractual quarterly payment schedule, a 2027 revenue forecast or near-term free cash flow. Cipher says deliveries are phased to the tenant's compute deployment, and the Q3 HPC revenue came from Black Pearl, a different campus.

The actual progression matters more than the headline total. At Black Pearl, rent began when capacity was delivered, and the company says additional halls there and at Barber Lake are scheduled to come online in phases through year-end. Each energized, accepted hall can change recognized rent. A delayed hall can postpone it. The next report needs to show the number of delivered halls or capacity, recognized HPC rent, project operating expense, and whether new debt or equity was needed to finish delivery. Without those pieces, a large multiyear agreement cannot be converted responsibly into a near-term stock price target.

Power rights and financing decide the 2027 branch

Cipher describes a roughly 5.9-gigawatt development pipeline. That is not the same thing as 5.9 gigawatts of energized, leased data centers. In the November 2 update, it reported conditional ERCOT classifications for 1 gigawatt at Colchis and an additional 1.6 gigawatts of studied load with provisional controllable-load designations. It has also begun lateral natural-gas pipeline development that it says could support up to 2.5 gigawatts of on-site generation. These are development steps with regulatory, construction, fuel-supply and financing conditions, not operating megawatts.

The company also identifies 270 megawatts potentially available in 2027 while it advances tenant discussions and design work. Available capacity is not a signed tenant. A bullish 2027 case requires timely power approvals, contracts, construction and rent commencement at attractive project economics. A base case would show steady rent growth but continued consolidated losses while the portfolio is built. A bearish case would see power or tenant delays combine with construction costs or financing pressure. These are conditional paths, not precise share-price forecasts; the disclosed inputs do not justify an honest dollar target today.

This makes dilution and capital structure part of the same forecast. The Q3 balance sheet lists 415.093 million common shares outstanding at September 30, versus 404.963 million at the end of 2025, a 2.5% increase. It also lists $5.447 billion of long-term borrowings and $0.656 billion of cash and equivalents, alongside $1.719 billion of restricted cash. Restricted cash is not interchangeable with freely available cash. Project-level debt may be supported by future rent, but common shareholders still need a clear bridge from completed campuses to cash after interest, maintenance and reinvestment.

What would change the CIFR forecast

The encouraging evidence is tangible: a first $5.852 million rent line, a low direct-cost line at this early stage and more capacity scheduled for delivery. TECHi’s CIFR quote page and forecast page provide dated market and analyst context, which should be kept separate from this filing-based operating test. The counterargument is equally tangible: mining sales fell 70.9% year over year, Q3 operating loss widened to $71.9 million, and reported net income benefited from a warrant revaluation rather than operating profit. The market's early decline does not settle which side wins over 2027. It signals that investors are demanding proof beyond the size of signed contracts.

For a constructive revision, watch for quarterly HPC rent rising toward the $17.3 million static adjusted-EBITDA hurdle and, over a longer period, for the operating-loss bridge to narrow without an equal jump in debt or shares. Those levels are TECHi sensitivities based on Q3 inputs, not company targets. A flat or falling rent line after promised hall deliveries, higher direct costs, weaker project margins or another delay in firm power access would weaken the thesis. An improving GAAP operating result together with cash generation would matter more than an isolated positive net-income print.

What to watch

The next dated test is Cipher's fourth-quarter 2026 results, expected in the next earnings cycle; the company has not provided a confirmed release date in this November 2 update. Before then, watch for disclosures on year-end data-hall delivery, ERCOT's final treatment of conditional load, and new tenant agreements for the 270 megawatts it identifies for 2027. The practical question for CIFR is whether each new megawatt becomes recognized rent and cash quickly enough to outrun the cost of building it.

data.title: Rohm lifts profit forecast 67%; depreciation drop matches 85% of H1 gain
data.description:
Rohm raised its annual operating-profit forecast by 66.7% on November 5, citing stronger AI-related server demand and improving profitability. The Japanese semiconductor maker now expects ¥50 billion for the year ending March 2027. But its newly released accounts show why investors should distinguish a recovery in reported profit from growth in earnings before depreciation.

TECHi calculates that the ¥8.389 billion decline in first-half depreciation was equivalent to 85.3% of the ¥9.834 billion increase in operating profit. Rohm’s own simplified EBITDA measure rose just 4.2%, against 128.5% growth in operating profit. That does not erase the genuine revenue recovery; it changes the test for whether the higher forecast represents a durable improvement in the business.

The upgrade is large, even after allowing for the accounting benefit

Rohm’s revised forecast covers April 1, 2026 through March 31, 2027. Expected revenue rises from ¥510 billion to ¥550 billion, an increase of 7.8%. Operating profit rises from ¥30 billion to ¥50 billion, while expected net profit attributable to owners increases from ¥29 billion to ¥45 billion. The revision was released through TDnet at 3:30 p.m. JST on November 5.

The difference between the two outlooks is ¥20 billion of operating profit against ¥40 billion of additional revenue. That 50% ratio is a comparison of forecast revisions, not a disclosed margin on individual products or proof that half of every future sales yen becomes profit. It captures a broader change in expected revenue, pricing, costs and business mix over the same fiscal year.

Rohm says server and storage demand remains strong as generative AI drives data-center investment. It also points to recovering factory-automation demand, resilient electrified-vehicle business, pricing initiatives and cost reductions. Management expects profitability to improve more than originally assumed, despite higher material, energy and logistics costs. The disclosure therefore describes a company-wide recovery with an AI contribution, rather than a business whose entire forecast can be assigned to AI chips.

The annual operating margin implied by the new outlook is 9.1%, compared with 5.9% in the previous plan. That 3.2-percentage-point increase is the practical promise investors need to assess. A larger market opportunity helps, but the forecast also requires Rohm to retain more profit from its sales.

What the 85% depreciation comparison actually measures

The first-half earnings report shows operating profit increasing from ¥7.653 billion to ¥17.487 billion. Depreciation expense in the cash-flow statement fell from ¥27.148 billion to ¥18.759 billion. Subtracting each pair produces the ¥9.834 billion profit increase and the ¥8.389 billion depreciation reduction used in TECHi’s calculation.

Dividing ¥8.389 billion by ¥9.834 billion gives 85.3%. This is an arithmetic bridge between two reported measures. It is not an estimate that 85% of customers’ purchases were artificial, nor does it establish that sales growth, pricing or restructuring had no economic value. It shows that most of the increase in profit after depreciation has a counterpart in a lower depreciation charge.

Rohm explicitly says that reduced depreciation following impairment charges in the previous fiscal year contributed to the first-half profit improvement. An impairment reduces the recorded value of assets; subsequent depreciation can then fall. The earlier write-down and the later expense reduction belong to different reporting periods, so reading only the latest operating-profit growth rate misses part of the story.

The company’s simplified EBITDA, defined as operating profit plus depreciation, was ¥36.247 billion, up 4.2%. Adding the published statement inputs, truncated to millions of yen, gives ¥36.246 billion; the ¥1 million difference reflects reporting precision. That small rounding difference does not change the conclusion: earnings before this expense increased much more slowly than operating profit.

The strongest counterargument is that a lower future cost base can still support shareholder returns. A past impairment does not make today’s reported profit unusable. But a stock forecast built on continued 128.5% operating-profit growth would need evidence beyond an expense reduction that has already occurred. EBITDA is also not cash flow: it excludes working-capital movements and does not fund factories by itself.

Server demand is real, but one major segment still loses money

First-half revenue rose 14.4% to ¥279.483 billion. Within the LSI business, Rohm reports strong server-related product growth alongside gains in automotive and industrial applications. Segment revenue increased 12.8% to ¥128.803 billion, and segment profit rose 35.5% to ¥17.556 billion.

The semiconductor devices business offers a more complicated picture. Revenue increased 20.7% to ¥120.720 billion. Rohm describes firm server demand for silicon-carbide power devices and a large increase in server-related silicon power-device sales. Nevertheless, the segment recorded a ¥4.393 billion loss, compared with a ¥9.809 billion loss a year earlier.

The loss narrowed by ¥5.416 billion, a meaningful improvement. It also means that higher sales have not yet produced profitability across this entire segment. Treating stronger AI infrastructure demand as proof that the silicon-carbide business has completed its turnaround would go beyond the results. Rohm continues to identify improving that business’s profitability as an objective.

Elsewhere, modules revenue fell 4.4% to ¥16.392 billion and segment profit declined 30.0% to ¥1.701 billion. The recovery is uneven. Neither the LSI result nor the semiconductor devices result should be presented as a separate AI revenue total, because the company’s reporting categories include several end markets.

For readers comparing Japanese suppliers, TECHi’s Shibaura forecast analysis examines a different issue: converting a much larger equipment order book into recognized revenue. Rohm’s fresh accounts instead make the relationship between depreciation, operating profit and cash generation central to the investment question.

The cash balance rose while operating cash flow fell

Rohm ended September with ¥477.535 billion of cash and cash equivalents, an increase of ¥48.821 billion from March-end. That provides substantial financial resources, but the cash-flow statement does not show that the increase came entirely from stronger trading.

Operating cash inflow declined to ¥25.546 billion from ¥47.190 billion a year earlier, a fall of 45.9%. The statement records a ¥23.331 billion working-capital outflow from receivables and a ¥17.122 billion inflow from trade payables. Those movements help explain why improved reported earnings did not translate into a similar increase in operating cash generation.

Investment activity provided ¥38.488 billion of net cash, including ¥62.754 billion from sales and redemptions of securities and investment securities. Meanwhile, purchases of property, plant and equipment fell to ¥26.682 billion from ¥81.624 billion.

A narrow cash-after-capex calculation is useful here: operating cash flow minus cash purchases of property, plant and equipment was negative ¥1.136 billion, compared with negative ¥34.434 billion a year earlier. This is TECHi’s explicitly defined calculation, not a company free-cash-flow forecast. It excludes securities transactions, subsidies and other investing items. It shows a much smaller funding gap, helped by sharply lower capital spending, while avoiding the assumption that asset sales are recurring operating income.

The balance sheet also lists ¥100 billion of short-term borrowing, ¥100 billion of long-term borrowing and ¥200 billion of bonds. Subtracting those ¥400 billion of financing balances from cash and cash equivalents leaves ¥77.535 billion. That limited comparison excludes other liabilities and is not a measure of cash available for an immediate distribution.

A stock forecast needs the right earnings denominator

At publication, the fixed price used for valuation is Rohm’s November 5 Tokyo close of ¥3,246 at 3:30 p.m. JST, from Yahoo Finance market data. Tokyo’s regular cash session has ended. The provider’s formal delay is unknown. The close was 6.0% below November 4’s ¥3,455, but its timestamp coincides with the disclosure time, so this daily move is not a clean measurement of the market’s response to the new forecast.

The company’s new annual basic EPS forecast is ¥116.56, compared with ¥75.12 previously. At the fixed closing price, that implies 27.8 times company-guidance earnings, versus 43.2 times using the previous forecast at the same price. These are company estimates for the year ending March 2027, not analyst consensus or a normalized earnings valuation.

If actual EPS were 20% below the new estimate, the multiple at an unchanged share price would rise to 34.8 times. That is a sensitivity, not a prediction of a miss or a share-price target. It illustrates how much the apparent valuation improvement depends on achieving the upgraded earnings denominator.

Share structure adds another limitation. Rohm reported first-half basic EPS of ¥40.36 and diluted EPS of ¥34.42. Those measures should not be interchanged, and the company’s annual basic forecast should not be described as a fully diluted estimate. Nor should the prior fiscal year’s large net loss be used to manufacture a meaningful positive trailing P/E.

What would strengthen or weaken the recovery case

The constructive case rests on more than depreciation. Server-related revenue is expanding, the semiconductor devices loss has narrowed, and the annual operating margin target has increased. Evidence that pricing and cost initiatives lift profitability while operating cash flow improves would make the recovery more convincing.

The weaker case would be revenue growth that leaves the power-device segment loss-making and fails to improve cash conversion. Currency also matters: the revised outlook assumes ¥153 per dollar for the second half. A different exchange-rate outcome, higher input costs or weaker automotive and industrial demand could alter the result. The release does not provide enough information to assign a precise stock-price effect to any one of these risks.

What to watch

Rohm says it plans to publish its earnings presentation and supplementary materials on November 6, followed by its semiannual securities report on November 9. The presentation is the next dated opportunity to assess the profit bridge, server demand and restructuring detail. Until those materials arrive, the useful forecast question is whether stronger demand produces growth in earnings and cash beyond the benefit of lower depreciation.

data.title: Ferrotec stock forecast: 33% profit upgrade waits for Nov. 4 open
data.description:
Ferrotec raised its nine-month 2026 operating-profit forecast to ¥68 billion from ¥60 billion and its net-profit forecast to ¥48 billion from ¥36 billion in a Tokyo exchange filing released at 5:30 p.m. Japan time on November 2. The Japanese semiconductor supplier attributed the upgrade to stronger demand for AI-related chipmaking components and thermal modules used in optical transceivers for data centers. Revenue guidance rose only 5.3%, to ¥400 billion, while the net-profit estimate climbed 33.3%.

That imbalance is the investment story. Ferrotec is now expecting a larger share of each additional yen of sales to reach operating profit, but investors have not yet had a normal cash-market session to price the new guidance. The announcement followed Monday's Tokyo close, and the Japan Exchange Group calendar shows the exchange closed Tuesday, November 3, for Culture Day. Wednesday, November 4, is the first regular-session test of whether the margin improvement changes the stock's outlook.

The upgrade is bigger than the sales increase

The revised forecast covers April 1 through December 31, 2026, a nine-month transition period as Ferrotec changes its fiscal year-end. The new ¥400 billion sales target is ¥20 billion above the August forecast of ¥380 billion. Operating profit rises ¥8 billion, or 13.3%, to ¥68 billion. Ordinary profit rises ¥11 billion, or 20%, to ¥66 billion. Profit attributable to the parent rises ¥12 billion, or 33.3%, to ¥48 billion. These are company forecasts, not booked results; each figure comes from the one-page revision notice.

The arithmetic exposes what the headline percentage can hide. The operating margin implied by the new guidance is 17.0%: ¥68 billion divided by ¥400 billion. The previous guide implied 15.8%: ¥60 billion divided by ¥380 billion. That is a gain of about 1.2 percentage points, not 1.2% of revenue. The incremental operating profit of ¥8 billion divided by incremental sales of ¥20 billion implies a 40% incremental operating margin on the revision. It is a sensitivity calculated from two forecasts, not a disclosed margin for a product line or evidence that future orders will carry the same economics.

The net-profit change deserves separate treatment. The ¥12 billion increase is larger than the ¥8 billion operating-profit increase because other lines and updated tax assumptions also matter. Ferrotec says it refreshed its consolidated tax forecast. It would be wrong to credit the entire 33.3% net-income uplift to higher-margin AI hardware. The company has not given a dollar or yen breakdown of the ceramics, quartz, vacuum components, metal processing and optical-transceiver thermal modules behind the revision.

An old 2027 plan now looks too small, with a major caveat

A second calculation puts the revision in context. In its May 2026 medium-term plan, Ferrotec set fiscal 2027 sales of ¥400 billion and operating profit of ¥48 billion. Its newly revised nine-month 2026 guidance calls for the same sales and ¥20 billion more operating profit. The 2026 operating-profit estimate is about 42% above that older 2027 plan: ¥20 billion divided by ¥48 billion.

This does not mean Ferrotec has formally upgraded its 2027 guidance, or that a nine-month period can be compared directly with a 12-month year. The old plan is a dated benchmark, and the current 2026 period is unusual. The useful finding is narrower: the company has revised near-term profit faster than it has revised its longer-range targets. Monday's notice says management will watch subsequent performance before reconsidering and disclosing any changes to the medium-term plan. That pending decision is a genuine forecast catalyst, rather than a target investors should assume has already moved.

The calendar mismatch also makes conventional growth comparisons hazardous. Ferrotec's March 2026 year had 12 months, while the December 2026 transition has nine. A simple comparison of ¥400 billion in the shorter guide with ¥288.9 billion of sales in the preceding 12-month year would suggest spectacular growth, but it mixes different reporting lengths. The company itself does not present a year-on-year percentage in the transition-period financial-results materials. A fair assessment needs the next reported half-year figures and segment detail, not a mechanically annualized headline.

Where AI enters Ferrotec's numbers

Ferrotec identifies two different demand paths. Its semiconductor-equipment business sells materials and components, including ceramics, quartz, vacuum seals and metal-processing work, for machinery used in chip production. Its electronics business supplies thermal modules for optical transceivers used in AI data centers. The company's optical-transceiver product page describes thermal-control components for links progressing from 800G to 1.6T and beyond. Those product descriptions explain the technical connection to AI infrastructure; they do not disclose customer identities or the revenue contribution from any specific data-center project.

The difference matters for a stock forecast. TECHi's Tokyo Electron profit test and Lasertec versus SCREEN comparison examined other links in Japan's AI equipment chain; Ferrotec supplies components rather than the same finished tools. Readers can also follow Ferrotec on its stock page. Chipmaking-equipment demand depends on capital spending by semiconductor manufacturers and their tool suppliers. Thermal modules for optical links depend on deployment of faster data-center networks. Both may benefit from AI spending, but they have different order cycles and potential bottlenecks. A good quarter in one business cannot automatically be extended to the other. Ferrotec's announcement says demand has strengthened in both groups and that the mix of more profitable products has improved since the prior forecast. It does not say how much of the ¥20 billion sales revision came from each business.

This leaves investors with a question that the next results can answer: is the 17% group operating margin supported by repeatable orders and a durable mix, or by a favorable period that could normalize? The risk is not merely that AI demand weakens. Costs of new capacity, pricing, customer concentration and the speed of optical-network deployment could all affect how much of today's incremental profit persists. The company's earlier analyst briefing Q&A described a Malaysian factory still ramping up; new manufacturing capacity can create a lag between sales opportunities and profit. That older observation is context, not proof of a current problem.

What the stock can and cannot tell us yet

Ferrotec closed at ¥7,676 on Monday, November 2, up ¥10 from Friday's ¥7,666 close, according to Kabutan's dated daily price record. Both prices are Japanese yen per share from the regular Tokyo session, before the 5:30 p.m. guidance release. Monday's 0.13% rise is therefore not a market verdict on the new announcement. Any after-hours indications would need their own venue, time and liquidity context; they cannot replace Wednesday's regular-session observation.

The revised earnings-per-share guide is ¥912.67, versus ¥683.66 previously. At Monday's pre-announcement close, the stock price divided by the new nine-month EPS estimate is about 8.4 times. That number is useful only as a transparent snapshot, not an ordinary 12-month price/earnings ratio. The numerator is a price before the news, the denominator is management's unearned forecast for a nine-month transition period, and the period does not match standard trailing or forward annual earnings. Using it as proof that the stock is cheap would create false precision.

A more defensible framework is to watch two separate tests. The first is market acceptance: does the November 4 regular-session price rise, hold and trade with meaningful volume once investors can react? The second is operating delivery: do the coming statements show that the revised sales and margin trajectory is being achieved? The stock can rally even if a forecast is later cut, or fall despite improved guidance if expectations were higher. Price action alone will not identify which product generated the upgrade.

For a bounded scenario, a 5% move from the November 2 close would equal about ¥384 a share, or a price near ¥8,060 on the upside and ¥7,292 on the downside. These are arithmetic markers, not targets or probabilities, and they say nothing about a fair value. They help readers distinguish an actual trading response from a claimed one. A sustained move should be evaluated against the revised earnings, the quality of the margin change and whatever management discloses next, not against a single percentage threshold.

The strongest counterargument

The bullish interpretation is that a supplier serving two AI infrastructure bottlenecks has enough pricing or mix strength to lift profit much faster than revenue. There is evidence for that in management's revised guidance and in the implied incremental margin. The strongest counterargument is that the disclosure provides no segment-level bridge, no order-book quantification and no revised 2027 plan. A one-page forecast cannot establish how much of the upgrade is recurring. It also arrives after a volatile run in the shares: Friday's close was below Thursday's ¥8,260, according to the same dated price series. That makes the reaction harder to interpret as a clean referendum on the filing.

A confirmation would be reported half-year sales, operating margin and business-line commentary that support the ¥400 billion and ¥68 billion full-transition-year targets. A disconfirmation would be weaker conversion of equipment orders into sales, less profitable mix, or a tax outcome that narrows the net-profit upgrade. Investors should also watch whether management replaces the older medium-term plan with a new one. Until that happens, the 42% gap between the new near-term operating-profit guide and the old 2027 target is a signal that assumptions need updating, not a company-issued 2027 forecast.

What to watch

The first observable regular-session response comes Wednesday, November 4, after Japan's November 3 market holiday. Ferrotec's investor calendar lists its mid-year financial-results announcement for November 16, 2026. That report should allow a better check of sales conversion and operating margin. The next important disclosure is any formal update to the medium-term plan. Those events, rather than a mechanical 33% stock-price extrapolation from the net-profit revision, will determine whether today's AI-linked margin story holds up.

data.title: Tempus AI stock hits $80.62 as data growth sets 2027 forecast
data.description:
Tempus AI shares touched $80.62 during Monday's U.S. session, 11.6% above Friday's $72.22 close, after the company reported $411.5 million of third-quarter revenue, up 23% from a year earlier. In its November 2 earnings release, the precision-medicine company raised the lower end of its 2026 sales outlook to $1.60 billion while holding the upper end at $1.605 billion. The intraday high is a dated observation, not a closing price or proof that any one line in the release caused the move.

The more useful stock question is whether the pieces that could lift 2027 sales are becoming large enough to justify the reaction. Tempus's faster-growing Data & Applications unit supplied only about 26% of third-quarter sales, but about 35% of the year's $77.3 million increase in quarterly revenue. Management also projects an approximately $80 million reimbursement benefit in 2027 from its xT CDx assay. Those are different growth engines, and the guidance revision itself was much smaller than the headline might suggest.

The $2.5 million guidance lift versus the 2027 question

Tempus's new 2026 revenue range of $1.600 billion to $1.605 billion compares with the $1.595 billion to $1.605 billion range in its second-quarter outlook. The high end did not move. The midpoint increased from $1.600 billion to $1.6025 billion, a $2.5 million change, or roughly 0.16% of the old midpoint. Tempus left its full-year adjusted EBITDA expectation at approximately $65 million. Calling this a substantial guidance reset would overstate what changed.

The company nevertheless beat the revenue level it had set for the September quarter. Its Q2 presentation guided to $405 million to $410 million for Q3; the reported $411.537 million exceeded the top end by $1.537 million. Adjusted EBITDA of $25.572 million also came in above its $15 million to $20 million quarterly target. These are concrete execution positives. They say little by themselves about whether the share price at its intraday high is reasonable, because a stock reflects many future years of expectations, not one beat.

There is an immediate fourth-quarter hurdle inside the full-year range. Tempus reported about $1.142 billion of revenue for the first nine months in its quarterly filing. Subtracting that from the new full-year guide implies roughly $458 million to $463 million of Q4 revenue. That is about 11% to 12% above Q3's $411.5 million, before rounding. This is TECHi's arithmetic from company figures, not a separate management forecast. The next report needs to show that sequential step, not merely another good year-on-year percentage.

The data business is small enough to grow fast and large enough to matter

The CEO and CFO letter gives the cleanest segment comparison. Data & Applications revenue rose from $81.3 million in Q3 2025 to $108.1 million in Q3 2026, a $26.8 million increase. Total company revenue rose from $334.206 million to $411.537 million, or $77.331 million. Dividing $26.8 million by $77.331 million shows the data unit supplied about 34.7% of the total revenue increase, despite representing only 26.3% of current quarterly sales.

That does not mean every Data & Applications dollar is an AI software subscription. The segment includes data licensing and modeling, applications and a service-oriented Trials business. The letter says Insights, its licensing and modeling activity, grew 29% year over year, while Applications contributed $9.7 million versus $3.2 million a year earlier. A faster segment mix is favorable, but treating the entire $108.1 million as recurring AI-platform revenue would make the stock story less accurate.

The mix also matters for profitability. Tempus reported a 72% GAAP gross margin for Data & Applications and 62% for Diagnostics in Q3. At the reported segment sales, a dollar shifting toward the higher-margin data unit can raise consolidated gross profit, all else equal. The company-wide GAAP gross profit of $266.7 million was 64.8% of revenue, up from $209.9 million a year ago. Tempus attributed the improvement to Data & Applications growth, reimbursement and lab efficiencies; no single factor can be isolated from the public figures with precision.

Bookings are an additional signal, not earned sales. Tempus said its data-licensing bookings exceeded $550 million year to date after its Bristol Myers Squibb collaboration. The letter describes two BMS-related agreements totaling up to $192.5 million over roughly five years and says their revenue should be recognized largely over that period, about $36 million annually on a go-forward basis, excluding any extra cloud or compute purchases. An investor who drops the whole booking amount into a 2027 revenue model would overstate the near-term contribution. The test is how these commitments convert into recognized revenue and gross profit quarter by quarter.

A 2027 sensitivity with two separate levers

Here is a bounded way to test the 2027 story without inventing a share-price target. If Data & Applications repeated its 33% year-on-year Q3 growth rate in the corresponding quarter of 2027, $108.1 million would become about $143.8 million, an increase of $35.7 million. Management separately expects its xT CDx pricing change to add approximately $80 million of average-selling-price benefit in 2027 after revised reimbursement takes effect on January 1. Spread evenly for illustration, that is $20 million per quarter, equal to about 6.6% of Q3 2026 Diagnostics revenue.

Together, those two isolated levers would be about $55.7 million of additional quarterly revenue on a Q3-sized base, or roughly 13.5% of Q3 2026 consolidated revenue. This is not a 2027 company forecast. The data growth rate may change; the pricing benefit is management's expectation, not cash already received; a calendar-year amount need not arrive evenly; and other Diagnostics changes, acquisitions and contract schedules also affect reported revenue. The point is to show how much of the possible next leg can be described with disclosed inputs, and which assumptions must be checked later.

A conservative countercase matters as much as the upside. Data & Applications grew 33% in Q3, but the company says its Trials component had softer growth. If licensing implementations slip, the same bookings could support revenue much later than stockholders expect. Likewise, the xT pricing benefit assumes successful conversion of tests to the higher-reimbursed assay on the timetable management described. A planned acquisition of Personalis could change both segment mix and cost structure; it is not included in this simple bridge. A one-quarter acceleration cannot establish a durable 2027 growth rate.

The stronger case is visible too. Oncology testing volumes grew 32% year over year, even as Diagnostics revenue grew 20%. Tempus says expanded reimbursement should help its realized price in 2027, and management reported roughly 12,000 minimal-residual-disease tests in Q3, up about 300%. Those volumes may create more clinical data that can support licensing and models over time. But the feedback loop is a business thesis, not a measured dollar of future revenue. Investors need subsequent test volumes, reimbursement receipts and segment sales to see whether it is actually compounding.

Adjusted profit is progress; GAAP still has distance to travel

Tempus's $25.572 million of adjusted EBITDA was its strongest disclosed quarterly figure, up from $1.476 million a year earlier. The company also reported $9.2 million of cash provided by operations in Q3 versus $7.5 million used in Q2. Those improvements are material and give the bull case something more solid than a contract announcement. The Q3 cash number, however, is one quarter, not a guarantee that full-year or post-acquisition cash generation is positive.

GAAP tells a more demanding story. The same earnings statement showed a $56.864 million operating loss and a $14.851 million net loss. The net loss narrowed from $79.982 million a year earlier, but included $42.8 million of unrealized gains on marketable securities. It also included $50.8 million of stock-based compensation and related payroll taxes. Neither item can simply be ignored: the unrealized gain can reverse, and stock compensation is an economic cost to shareholders even when adjusted metrics exclude it.

The arithmetic gap between the $266.701 million gross profit and $323.565 million GAAP operating expenses was $56.864 million. A hypothetical extra $87.8 million of quarterly sales at the quarter's 64.8% blended gross margin could close that operating gap if all other costs and margins stayed fixed. That assumption is unlikely to hold perfectly as Tempus expands testing, invests in models or integrates Personalis. It is a sensitivity, not a claim that the company needs exactly $87.8 million next quarter or that Q4 guidance produces GAAP profit. It makes the remaining scale issue visible beside the adjusted EBITDA headline.

Cash and marketable securities ended September at $854.4 million, according to the release. That is a useful financing buffer but not a substitute for comparing operating cash flow and acquisition spending over multiple quarters. The stock's reaction can reasonably reflect improving margins and cash conversion. It can also reverse if the 2027 reimbursement benefit arrives slowly or the data unit's higher growth fails to translate into earnings after operating expense.

What the share move can and cannot say

The market quote showed TEM at $78.82 at 10:46 a.m. Eastern, up 9.1% from the prior close, after it had touched $80.62 during the session. The high occurred in the preceding hour, around 10:46 a.m. on an intraday price feed. That confirms a meaningful same-day reaction; it does not reveal whether traders were responding mainly to revenue, adjusted EBITDA, the 2027 reimbursement expectation, broader health-technology buying or some mixture of them. The high also should not be read as a price target.

For a 2027 stock forecast, the key distinction is between a limited near-term guidance lift and a potentially larger but unproven next-year revenue bridge. Q4 must deliver the roughly $458 million to $463 million implied by current guidance. Data & Applications must keep contributing a disproportionate share of growth without weakening its margin. Reimbursement gains must appear in realized Diagnostics revenue. If those three checks hold while GAAP operating losses continue to narrow, the case for a higher valuation becomes stronger. If any one stalls, Monday's intraday enthusiasm could prove premature.

What to watch

The next dated checkpoint is Personalis' November 30 shareholder meeting on the proposed transaction; Tempus says regulatory review has cleared, but shareholder approval and other closing conditions remain. Then watch the fourth-quarter results for the $458 million to $463 million revenue implication of the current full-year guide, the first reported effect of January 1 reimbursement pricing, and whether Data & Applications growth remains ahead of the company as a whole. These are the numbers that can test the 2027 case more reliably than a single day's high.

data.title: Shibaura raises profit forecast to ¥17.5B; H2 needs an 85% jump
data.description:
Shibaura Mechatronics raised its annual operating-profit forecast to ¥17.5 billion on November 5, citing stronger semiconductor investment. Yet the Japanese chip-equipment maker must earn ¥11.356 billion in the October–March half to deliver that target: almost 85% more than it earned in April–September, according to TECHi’s calculation from its newly released results.

The forecast revision, published at 3 p.m. JST, strengthens the company’s AI-equipment growth case without resolving its delivery risk. Orders almost doubled, but first-half operating profit fell. For investors assessing Shibaura’s stock, the important question is how quickly those orders become revenue at the higher margin the new forecast requires.

A higher forecast with most profit still to come

For the year ending March 31, 2027, Shibaura now expects revenue of ¥105 billion, up from ¥99 billion, and operating profit of ¥17.5 billion, up from ¥16 billion. Those are increases of 6.1% and 9.4% from its previous forecasts. Expected net profit rises more modestly, to ¥12.5 billion from ¥11.9 billion.

The starting point is mixed. The April–September earnings report shows revenue of ¥43.216 billion, up 2.2% from a year earlier, alongside operating profit of ¥6.144 billion, down 18.9%. Net profit attributable to owners fell 19.6% to ¥4.275 billion. A higher full-year target therefore depends on a recovery that has yet to appear in the reported half-year totals.

Subtracting the first-half results from the annual forecast leaves ¥61.784 billion of second-half revenue and ¥11.356 billion of operating profit. Revenue must increase 43.0% from the first half; operating profit must increase 84.8%. Nearly 65% of the year’s forecast operating profit remains to be earned after September.

The required margin is equally revealing. First-half operating profit divided by revenue gives 14.2%. The implied second-half margin is 18.4%, an improvement of about 4.2 percentage points. That is consistent with the company’s rounded second-half presentation, but the exact subtraction exposes the scale of the acceleration more clearly than the annual upgrade alone.

This does not establish that management’s forecast is unrealistic. Equipment shipments can be uneven, and Shibaura identifies work moving into later periods. It does mean that stronger bookings alone are insufficient confirmation. The forecast needs both a substantial revenue step and improved profitability on that revenue.

AI orders provide the strongest counterargument

The most persuasive support for the raised outlook is the order book. Shibaura reported ¥79.124 billion of first-half orders, up 92.3% from a year earlier. Against ¥43.216 billion of revenue, that is a book-to-bill ratio of 1.83 times: orders received during the period were about 83% greater than sales recognized during it.

Its results presentation puts the September-end backlog at ¥84.2 billion. That exceeds the ¥61.784 billion of revenue needed in the second half. The comparison supports the view that demand exists, but backlog is not a promise that every order will ship, meet revenue-recognition conditions and become revenue before March 31. The disclosed total does not provide a complete delivery calendar.

The AI connection is explicit in the company’s account of semiconductor back-end demand. Management says advanced-packaging equipment orders increased sharply on generative-AI demand. Its Mechatronics Systems segment, which also includes display back-end and vacuum applications, booked ¥45.607 billion of orders, up 195.4%. Segment revenue rose 12.0% to ¥19.411 billion, while operating profit increased 15.0% to ¥5.406 billion.

That segment’s orders were 2.35 times its revenue, using the same first-half period. The difference between booking growth and sales growth helps explain the opportunity: much of the commercial momentum has not yet reached reported revenue. It also explains the timing risk. Investors should not treat a signed equipment order as earnings already earned.

Nor should they label the entire segment AI revenue. The company groups several businesses together and does not disclose a separate AI-sales total in these results. Generic references to GPU-related demand do not identify a specific customer or justify assigning the order increase to one American chip designer.

The recovery also needs the weaker business

Shibaura’s Fine Mechatronics segment presents the other side of the forecast. First-half revenue fell 2.9% to ¥21.968 billion, and segment operating profit declined 54.9% to ¥1.420 billion. Orders nevertheless increased 35.2% to ¥31.700 billion.

Management attributes the semiconductor front-end revenue weakness partly to customer investment-plan reviews and delivery-schedule changes that shifted some sales into the second half or later. It describes those timing effects as temporary and says overall progress was broadly according to plan. That is management’s assessment, rather than independent confirmation that all deferred work will be recognized this fiscal year.

Depreciation from growth investment also weighed on profit. The presentation forecasts ¥21.8 billion of combined personnel, research-and-development and depreciation costs for the year, up from its previous ¥21.3 billion plan. Higher revenue needs to absorb an expanding cost base, which makes execution more important than a simple order-growth extrapolation suggests.

The segment comparison favors the back-end equipment business on current growth and profitability. It does not show that the group can ignore front-end weakness. The two main segment profit figures also cannot be added and treated as consolidated operating profit without the other businesses and adjustments in the group accounts.

For context, TECHi’s Advantest–Tokyo Electron comparison examines different profit requirements across Japanese chip-equipment companies. Shibaura’s new results present a distinct issue: unusually strong order intake alongside a substantial second-half recovery requirement.

Cash improved, but customer advances matter

Shibaura’s first-half cash generation looks much stronger than its earnings. Operating cash inflow was ¥32.778 billion and investing cash outflow was ¥3.385 billion. The company defines their combined ¥29.393 billion inflow as free cash flow. Cash and cash equivalents reached ¥46.729 billion at September 30.

The balance sheet explains why that cash improvement should be interpreted carefully. Advances received from customers increased by ¥21.110 billion from March-end; the September balance was ¥24.797 billion. These payments support liquidity and demonstrate customer commitments, but they accompany future delivery obligations. Receiving cash early is different from completing a profitable sale.

The presentation itself provides a useful warning against annualizing the first-half inflow. Management forecasts approximately ¥18.5 billion of full-year free cash flow, comprising ¥29.4 billion in the first half and a ¥10.9 billion outflow in the second. The expected reversal is consistent with using cash to fulfill orders after receiving advance payments.

There is financial capacity behind that work. The September balance sheet lists ¥7.6 billion of short-term borrowing and ¥0.9 billion of long-term borrowing due within one year. Cash exceeds those borrowing balances, although the company also has leases and other liabilities. Its equity ratio fell to 47.6% from 55.1% at March-end as the balance sheet expanded. Calling all of the cash surplus distributable would overlook the obligations supporting it.

What the new earnings forecast means for valuation

At publication, the fixed market observation used here is ¥2,421 at 3:07:33 p.m. JST on November 5, supplied by Yahoo Finance market data. This was a Tokyo regular-session observation; the provider’s formal delay is unknown. Against the November 4 close of ¥3,035, it represents a 20.2% decline. It is not a live quote or the November 5 closing price, and the daily decline cannot be attributed entirely to the earnings release.

Shibaura’s revised company forecast is ¥190.32 of earnings per share for the year ending March 2027, compared with its previous ¥181.29 estimate. At the fixed ¥2,421 observation, the new forecast implies a price-to-earnings multiple of 12.7 times, versus 13.4 times using the old estimate at that same price. Those are company-guidance multiples, not analyst consensus or normalized earnings measures.

The company’s March 1, 2026 five-for-one share split matters when comparing historical figures. The EPS values in the revision notice are presented on the adjusted share basis. Mixing them with an old unsplit share price would produce a misleading valuation.

The sensitivity table changes earnings while holding the share price constant. It is not a price-target model. If earnings undershoot the new forecast by 10%, the apparent multiple rises to 14.1 times; a 20% shortfall takes it to 15.9 times. A low-looking forward multiple is less persuasive when the denominator depends on a large unfinished profit step.

The dividend forecast increases from ¥64 to ¥67 per share, all expected at fiscal year-end. At the fixed price that implies a prospective 2.77% yield, conditional on the payout being made. It does not offset a possible capital loss or establish a floor under the stock.

What would change the forecast assessment

The constructive case is concrete: a larger backlog, strong advanced-packaging demand and customer advances give Shibaura resources and booked business with which to pursue its raised target. Evidence that delayed front-end shipments are becoming recognized sales, while back-end profitability holds up, would strengthen that case.

The adverse case is equally specific. Delivery slippage into the following fiscal year, weaker equipment mix or a slower margin recovery could prevent revenue growth from translating into the required profit. Management also flags semiconductor export restrictions and longer component lead times. These risks matter because the annual forecast assumes improvement during a limited remaining delivery window.

The most useful forecast is therefore an execution test rather than an unsupported target for the share price. Track second-half revenue against ¥61.784 billion, operating profit against ¥11.356 billion and margin against roughly 18.4%. A change in those underlying prospects would matter more than mechanically applying a preferred earnings multiple.

What to watch

Shibaura plans to file its semiannual securities report on November 12, according to the earnings release. That is the next dated document checkpoint for the balance sheet and reporting detail. Through March 31, 2027, the central question remains whether the company can convert its AI-linked order surge into the higher sales and margin required by its newly raised forecast.

data.title: Tesla FSD referral offer rewards paid sign-ups; stock test is retention
data.description:
Tesla's October 29 referral offer is a small but revealing change to the stock story. Under terms effective that day, an eligible owner can give another Tesla owner a one-month trial of Full Self-Driving (Supervised). The referrer earns one free month of FSD or a $99 Tesla Credit only if the invitee buys a subscription during that trial. The incentive is aimed at turning cars already on the road into paying software accounts. That is a different commercial test from persuading somebody to buy a new vehicle.

The crucial number for investors is not how many trial links are shared. It is how many recipients become paying subscribers and how long they stay. Tesla has reported rising FSD adoption, but its much-cited 1.74 million active subscriptions at the end of the third quarter cannot answer that question. The company's Q3 update, in its own footnote, says the count includes people who paid upfront as well as monthly subscribers, while excluding free trials. Treating all 1.74 million as $99-a-month customers would therefore create a fictional recurring-revenue figure.

This is the original forecast test for Tesla stock: the new program should increase the monthly-paying base after the free month, at a cost that leaves attractive revenue after the reward. Tesla has not disclosed the program's conversion rate, paid-subscriber split or retention by cohort. A bullish or bearish price target based on those missing inputs would be false precision. The reported terms do, however, let investors define the evidence that would change the case.

What Tesla changed in the referral funnel

Tesla's program guide says a referrer must have an active FSD subscription or have bought the feature outright. An eligible recipient must own or lease a compatible Tesla, must not currently have FSD, and generally must not have used an FSD trial or subscription in the preceding 12 months. A one-year complimentary FSD grant does not qualify a referrer. The link must be generated and redeemed through the Tesla app. Availability depends on the markets Tesla has opened to the program; the terms do not make this a global offer to every Tesla owner.

The reward arrives only on a paid conversion during the one-month trial. A subscribing referrer gets a free month of FSD. An outright-purchase referrer can receive $99 in Tesla Credits, subject to eligible uses and expiry. The legal terms cap a referrer at 12 redeemed trials and 12 benefits per calendar year, and 48 benefits over the life of an account. Crucially, even a trial that produces no subscription consumes one of the annual trial slots. That makes the program more selective than an unlimited invitation scheme and means headline trial volume alone would overstate the economic opportunity.

The terms are also careful about the product: FSD is Supervised. Tesla's FSD support page lists a $99 U.S. monthly subscription and says pricing and availability can change. This referral initiative should not be read as evidence that a referred owner can operate a driverless robotaxi or that Tesla has obtained a new autonomy approval. It is a software-subscription sales channel for eligible vehicles.

The shift is strategically interesting because it reaches beyond a new-car checkout. Tesla's Q3 update reported over 75% FSD attach rate on new North American deliveries, a nearly 20-percentage-point sequential rise. The referral program asks existing FSD users to sell a trial to the installed fleet, including owners who are not in a dealership or ordering flow. Tesla has not disclosed the eligible size of that fleet, so its 10.2 million cumulative deliveries are not a usable denominator: those deliveries span years, markets, ownership changes, incompatible hardware and prior FSD purchases or trials.

The subscription metric investors cannot turn into sales

Tesla reported 1.48 million active FSD subscriptions at the end of Q2 and 1.74 million at the end of Q3. The increase of 260,000 is 17.6% sequentially; against 1.04 million a year earlier, the Q3 count is about 67% higher. The growth is meaningful as a measure of FSD access. It is not a count of 1.74 million customers paying $99 every month. Tesla's Q3 footnote explicitly combines upfront-payment users with monthly subscriptions and excludes free trials.

Multiplying 1.74 million by $99 and then by 12 gives roughly $2.07 billion. That arithmetic is useful only as an illustration of the mistake. It is not Tesla's disclosed FSD annual recurring revenue, and it is not even a reliable upper bound: some users paid upfront, some monthly prices or currencies differ, and timing and revenue recognition are not captured by that formula. The new free trials will not enter Tesla's reported active-subscription count until a recipient becomes a qualifying subscriber under the company's definition. Even then, the aggregate count does not reveal how many remain on a monthly plan.

The Q3 Form 10-Q gives another tempting but unusable shortcut. Tesla listed $4.08 billion of deferred revenue tied to internet connectivity, FSD access and ongoing maintenance, free Supercharging and software updates, up from $3.87 billion at the end of 2025. That is a bundled balance-sheet obligation, not an FSD subscription-revenue line. It cannot be divided by $99 to infer the number of paying FSD customers. The company said higher automotive ancillary sales in Q3 were primarily driven by increasing FSD subscriptions, which supports the direction of travel, but not a standalone dollar forecast for the referral plan.

TECHi's earlier Tesla Q3 cash-flow analysis examined the quarter's $1.53 billion free-cash-flow swing. The referral terms pose a different question: whether FSD can add durable, separately measurable software revenue without requiring another vehicle sale. Its October Slovakia rollout analysis explained why the FSD user count needs its footnote. The new U.S. referral funnel gives that distinction a practical test.

The $99 face-value hurdle

The offer has a simple unit-economics checkpoint, though it does not expose Tesla's actual costs. At the current advertised U.S. price, a referred user who buys one paid month generates $99 in gross billings. The successful referrer can earn a free month of the same service or a $99 credit. At face value, one paid month and one reward are equal. If that new customer stays for a second paid month, gross billings reach $198 against the reward's $99 face value, leaving $99 before service costs, taxes, promotions, unused credits and accounting differences. This is not a calculation of profit or customer-acquisition cost; a free month may have a different incremental cost from $99, and a credit may be redeemed against a purchase that otherwise would not have happened.

The free trial offered to the recipient matters as well. A trial that never converts brings no paid subscription and no referrer reward, but it may still incur operational cost and can occupy one of the referrer's annual trial slots. Conversely, a trial that persuades a long-retained customer to subscribe could create many months of billings. Without trial starts, conversion, cancellation rates and reward redemption, investors cannot decide which outcome dominates.

For scale, consider an explicitly illustrative cohort of 100,000 eligible trial redemptions in the United States. At 10% paid conversion, 10,000 users would start a $99 plan: $990,000 in one-month gross billings and up to $990,000 in reward face value. At 20% conversion, both figures double. If all converters then paid for six months, the 10% case would generate $5.94 million in six-month gross billings, still before the reward and costs. These figures are scenario arithmetic, not Tesla guidance or a prediction of how many owners will participate. They show why retention is more important than a large first-month trial count.

A Tesla stock forecast built around evidence, not trial hype

Base case: The referral program adds a new way to reach compatible owners, but its financial contribution remains unquantifiable from public data. Tesla's Q3 FSD access count can continue to grow without proving the same growth in monthly cash receipts. In this case, the stock's valuation still depends mostly on the broader vehicle, energy, autonomy and spending outlook rather than on an assumed windfall from referrals.

Upside case: Tesla discloses a rising number of monthly-paying FSD accounts, stronger retention after the free trial and a material contribution to automotive ancillary revenue. A repeatable program that brings owners into the subscription without a new vehicle purchase would strengthen the software margin argument. The most convincing evidence would be a consistent series of paid-account and net-retention figures, not app screenshots or a one-quarter jump in the blended FSD access count.

Downside case: Trial use rises while paid conversion is weak, or many recipients leave after one billed month. The face-value reward would then absorb most of the first-month billings per converter, and the aggregate active-FSD figure could still rise because of upfront users or other channels. A weaker outcome could also follow if market eligibility, compatible hardware or the 12-month exclusions leave a smaller prospect pool than promoters assume. These are falsifiable conditions, not a prediction that the program has already failed.

There is a fair counterargument to this cautious view. Tesla already has an engaged owner network, an in-app delivery channel and a product that can be activated on compatible cars without building another factory. A referral from an owner who actually uses FSD may convert better than a generic advertisement. The current terms also withhold the referrer's reward unless the recipient purchases a subscription, limiting rewards tied to unsuccessful trials. Those advantages are plausible; Tesla has not published the cohort data needed to put a value on them.

The next investor check should therefore be precise. Watch for a breakout of paying monthly FSD subscribers from upfront owners, the conversion and retention of referred trial users, and identifiable revenue or margin effects in future Tesla filings. Until then, the October 29 program is a potentially useful distribution experiment, not proof of a new recurring-revenue total. For Tesla stock, its most important result will be whether the company can turn interest in supervised driving into repeat payments after the introductory month.

data.title: Marvell-Lumentum stock forecast: $86 deal gap after midday lows
data.description:
Marvell and Lumentum shares both made new intraday lows around 12:46–12:47 p.m. Eastern on Monday, after the companies announced a $115 billion all-stock AI-connectivity merger. At 12:57 p.m., Marvell (MRVL) was about $177.48 and Lumentum (LITE) about $712.92 on synchronized one-minute price bars. The signed exchange ratio is 4.5 Marvell shares for each Lumentum share. That made the stock consideration worth about $798.65 at that moment, leaving Lumentum roughly $85.73, or 10.7%, below the then-current exchange value. These are intraday observations, not closing prices, a cash offer or a guaranteed return.

That gap is the more revealing stock story than the $1,132-per-share figure in the companies' November 2 announcement. The $1,132 was calculated from unaffected October 28 closing share prices, before merger speculation. The consideration floats with Marvell's share price until a transaction that is not expected to close until the first half of 2028. Monday's selloff reduced the current paper value of the 4.5-share promise, while Lumentum traded at a further discount to that lower value. TECHi's original calculation isolates those two separate effects.

The quoted deal value is a historical snapshot

Marvell's filed announcement and presentation describe an implied $115 billion enterprise value for Lumentum, an approximately $1,132 value per Lumentum share and a 23.9% premium using both companies' unaffected October 28 closes. The consideration, however, is not $1,132 in cash. It is a fixed exchange ratio of 4.500 Marvell shares. A buyer of Lumentum today would ultimately receive shares whose dollar value will depend on where MRVL trades when the merger closes, provided it closes at all.

The distinction is large because the buyer's stock has moved. At the paired 12:57 p.m. readings, 4.5 multiplied by $177.48 was $798.66. That is about $333 below the announcement's $1,132 reference value, or 29.4% lower. It does not mean Marvell cut the share ratio; it means the market price of the shares to be delivered is lower than the price embedded in the unaffected-date illustration. LITE then traded another $85.74 below the $798.66 value, taking it about 37.0% below the quoted $1,132 reference. An investor who calls that entire difference a takeover spread would be mixing two distinct changes.
